content.description: Phencyclidine (PCP) is a dissociative hallucinogen that was originally developed as an anesthetic. It produces a unique combination of stimulant, depressant, hallucinogenic, and dissociative effects. Use disorder involves a problematic pattern of PCP use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, while intoxication refers to recent use with characteristic behavioral and physical symptoms.

aeo.what_is: A pattern of problematic PCP use causing impairment, plus intoxication symptoms including aggression, unpredictability, and physical signs.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: Marcus, a 19-year-old college student, tries PCP at a party and becomes violently aggressive, attacking friends who try to calm him. He has no memory of the incident and wakes up in the hospital with injuries.

Sarah, 28, started using PCP occasionally at clubs but now finds herself using multiple times weekly. Her boyfriend notices she's become unpredictable and emotionally distant, switching from euphoria to paranoia within minutes.

David, a 35-year-old construction worker, uses PCP on weekends to feel 'invincible.' After breaking his hand punching a wall without feeling pain, he continues working for days before seeking medical attention.

Tasha, 22, experiments with what she thinks is marijuana but it's laced with PCP. She experiences terrifying hallucinations and becomes convinced people are trying to hurt her, barricading herself in a bathroom.

James, 41, has been using PCP for years and now experiences persistent cognitive problems. He struggles to remember conversations, loses track of time, and his family notices his personality has fundamentally changed.

Lisa, 25, uses PCP to cope with past trauma, finding the dissociative effects temporarily relieve her emotional pain. She's had three emergency room visits for bizarre behavior but continues using despite legal consequences.

Michael, 17, gets expelled from school after showing up intoxicated on PCP, exhibiting slurred speech and aggressive behavior. His parents had no idea he was using drugs until the school called the police.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Denial that PCP use is a serious problem, especially if intoxication episodes are infrequent
Fear of legal consequences or being labeled as violent or dangerous
Minimization of risks, claiming they can control their use or that effects are exaggerated
Shame about losing control during intoxication, particularly if violence or bizarre behavior occurred
Anxiety about withdrawal or life without the dissociative escape PCP provides
Confusion about why their behavior changes so dramatically when using PCP

first_person_statements: I didn't think it was a big deal until I woke up in the hospital with no memory of attacking my best friend. They said I was like a different person.
The worst part is not knowing what I'll do when I'm high. I've done things on PCP that I would never do sober, and people are scared of me now.
It felt like an out-of-body experience, like I was watching someone else live my life. That disconnection was exactly what I wanted, but now I can't connect even when I'm sober.
Everyone thinks PCP users are just violent criminals, but I used it to escape trauma. The diagnosis made me realize I was destroying myself trying to avoid pain.
I broke three bones while high on PCP and didn't feel any of it. Looking back, that numbness could have killed me, but at the time I felt powerful.
My family doesn't understand why I keep using despite everything that's happened. Neither do I, honestly. I just know the cravings are overwhelming.

mechanisms: PCP is a noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist, disrupting glutamate neurotransmission and causing dissociation.
It also influences dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin systems, contributing to psychosis-like symptoms and mood alterations.
High doses can affect multiple neurotransmitter systems, leading to severe agitation, delirium, and potential neurotoxicity.

diagnostic_criteria.use_disorder: At least 2 of 11 DSM-5 criteria within 12 months (e.g., taking larger amounts, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, craving, role impairment, continued use despite harm, tolerance).
diagnostic_criteria.intoxication: Recent PCP use, clinically significant problematic behavioral or psychological changes (e.g., belligerence, assaultiveness, impulsiveness, unpredictability, psychomotor agitation), plus at least two of: vertical or horizontal nystagmus, hypertension or tachycardia, numbness or decreased responsiveness to pain, ataxia, dysarthria, muscle rigidity, seizures or coma, hyperacusis.

content.temporal_criteria: Use disorder requires at least two symptoms occurring within a 12-month period showing a persistent pattern. Intoxication develops during or shortly after PCP use, with behavioral changes and physical signs appearing within minutes to hours. Symptoms typically resolve within 8-24 hours but can persist longer with high doses. Chronic use may cause lasting cognitive and psychiatric effects that continue beyond intoxication periods.
content.prevalence: Relatively uncommon compared to other substances; use is concentrated in certain regions and subcultures.
content.age_of_onset: Most often in adolescence or early adulthood.
content.prognosis: PCP intoxication can be life-threatening due to violent behavior, accidents, or severe medical complications; chronic use can cause persistent cognitive and mood disturbances.

history: Pattern and quantity of PCP use
History of violent or psychotic episodes
medical_workup: Toxicology screen (though PCP may not be included on standard panels)
Vital signs monitoring for hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia

environmental: Peer group tolerance of risky behavior

impact_on_life.social: Relationship strain due to aggression or erratic behavior
impact_on_life.occupational: Work or school disruptions from intoxication episodes

medications: No FDA-approved medications for PCP use disorder
Antipsychotics (haloperidol, atypicals) for severe psychosis, with caution due to seizure risk
care_coordination: Referral to substance use treatment programs

missed_diagnosis_factors: Aggressive or psychotic symptoms misattributed solely to primary psychiatric disorders
Negative toxicology screens if PCP is not specifically tested for
overdiagnosis_factors: Erratic behavior due to other hallucinogens or medical causes misclassified as PCP intoxication

misdiagnosis_explained.why_confusion_occurs: PCP intoxication produces severe psychotic symptoms, aggression, and bizarre behavior that closely mimics primary psychotic disorders. The dissociative and stimulant effects overlap with other substances. Without specific toxicology testing, PCP use may be missed entirely. Violent or agitated presentations may be attributed to psychiatric illness rather than substance intoxication.
clarifying_factors: Nystagmus (especially vertical) is characteristic of PCP but not typical in primary psychosis
Decreased pain sensitivity and unusual physical strength during episodes
Symptom onset is acute and time-linked to substance use rather than gradual deterioration
Specific toxicology testing for PCP (not always included in standard drug screens)
Physical signs like hypertension, tachycardia, and muscle rigidity during acute episodes
Complete or significant symptom resolution within hours to days, unlike persistent psychotic disorders

warning_signs: Sudden onset of aggression or violence without clear provocation
Reports of 'feeling invincible' or insensitive to pain
self_help_strategies: Avoid environments where PCP is present
Develop coping strategies for peer pressure

adults: More severe legal and occupational consequences

real_life_examples.title: The Party That Changed Everything
real_life_examples.baseline: Marcus was a 19-year-old college sophomore with a 3.5 GPA, active in intramural sports, and planning to major in business. He occasionally drank at parties but had never tried hard drugs. His friends knew him as easygoing and non-confrontational.
real_life_examples.first_change: At an off-campus party, someone offered him what they said was 'special weed.' Within 20 minutes of smoking it, Marcus felt completely detached from his body and became convinced his friends were trying to trap him. When his roommate approached to check on him, Marcus violently shoved him into a wall.
real_life_examples.behaviors: Marcus began swinging at anyone who came near him, his eyes showing distinctive rapid movements. He tried to jump through a second-story window, claiming he could fly. Friends reported he seemed to have superhuman strength and didn't react when he cut his hand badly on broken glass. His speech was slurred and he couldn't walk straight, stumbling into furniture. He alternated between aggressive outbursts and standing frozen, staring at nothing.
real_life_examples.consequences: Police were called when Marcus became uncontrollable. It took four officers to restrain him. He was hospitalized, where doctors noted vertical nystagmus, extremely elevated blood pressure, and muscle rigidity. A specialized toxicology screen revealed PCP. His roommate suffered a concussion from being pushed. Marcus was suspended from school pending a hearing.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Marcus has no memory of the incident beyond smoking the cigarette. He's facing assault charges, expelled from his dorm, and lost his scholarship. His former roommate won't speak to him. He's been diagnosed with PCP intoxication and is now in outpatient substance abuse treatment, though he's terrified about his legal future and struggles with guilt over hurting his friend. He's been advised that even one-time PCP use can have lasting consequences.

real_life_examples.title: Weekend Escape
real_life_examples.baseline: David, 35, worked construction six days a week to support his family. He dealt with chronic back pain and job stress but took pride in being a reliable provider. His wife described him as a quiet, hardworking man who rarely showed emotion but was devoted to their two kids.
real_life_examples.first_change: A coworker introduced him to PCP as a way to 'blow off steam' on Saturday nights. David found the dissociative effects allowed him to escape his worries and physical pain. For a few hours, he felt powerful and invincible. He began using PCP most weekends, then started using Thursday nights too.
real_life_examples.behaviors: During one episode, David became convinced he had superhuman strength and punched through a wooden fence, then punched a concrete wall, breaking three bones in his hand. He felt no pain and continued using the hand normally, telling his wife he'd 'tweaked it' at work. He showed up to work Monday with a massively swollen, purple hand but insisted on operating heavy machinery. Coworkers noticed him slurring words and moving erratically. His personality shifted on weekends—sometimes euphoric and grandiose, other times paranoid and aggressive. His wife noticed his eyes moving strangely.
real_life_examples.consequences: David finally went to urgent care when his hand became infected. X-rays showed multiple untreated fractures that had begun healing incorrectly. He was referred to the ER, where doctors recognized signs of PCP use. His employer was contacted due to safety concerns about operating equipment while impaired. He was placed on leave pending drug testing. The hand required surgery and months of recovery.
real_life_examples.aftermath: David is in intensive outpatient treatment and attending NA meetings, but the cravings are intense. His hand healed poorly, affecting his ability to do construction work. He's facing possible termination. His wife is considering separation, saying she doesn't recognize him anymore. David struggles with the realization that his 'escape' has destroyed the life he was trying to escape from, and he's working with a therapist on underlying pain management and stress coping strategies.

real_life_examples.title: Searching for Numbness
real_life_examples.baseline: Lisa, 25, was a sexual assault survivor who had tried multiple therapies for PTSD but continued experiencing severe flashbacks and emotional pain. She worked as a pharmacy technician and lived alone. Friends described her as increasingly withdrawn and struggling, though she maintained her job performance.
real_life_examples.first_change: Someone at a club offered her PCP, saying it would 'make everything go away.' The dissociative effect was unlike anything she'd experienced—she felt completely disconnected from her trauma and her body. For the first time in years, she felt relief from the constant emotional pain.
real_life_examples.behaviors: Lisa began using PCP several times weekly, seeking that dissociative state. During one episode at home, she became convinced people were breaking in and called 911, screaming that intruders were attacking her. Police found her barricaded in her bathroom, highly agitated and experiencing vivid hallucinations. She exhibited nystagmus and was barely responsive to questions. Another time, she showed up to work intoxicated, speaking incoherently and knocking over medication bottles. Her coordination was so impaired she nearly mixed up prescriptions. Coworkers noticed her pupils and eye movements looked abnormal, and her personality had become unpredictable—sometimes detached, sometimes paranoid.
real_life_examples.consequences: Lisa was terminated from her pharmacy position after the workplace incident and lost her certification. She's had three emergency room visits for PCP-related episodes. Her landlord is threatening eviction due to disturbances. She was arrested for disorderly conduct during one paranoid episode in public.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Lisa is now in a dual diagnosis program addressing both PTSD and substance use disorder. She's learning that she was essentially self-medicating trauma with a dangerous substance, but breaking the pattern is incredibly difficult. The dissociation felt like the only relief she could find. She's working with a trauma specialist on evidence-based PTSD treatments while managing intense cravings. Her criminal record and lost pharmacy certification have severely limited her career options, and she's struggling financially while trying to maintain recovery.

real_life_examples.title: Years of Use, Lasting Changes
real_life_examples.baseline: James, 41, had been using PCP on and off since his early twenties. He'd held various jobs and had periods of sobriety but would return to PCP during stressful times. His family had noticed cognitive changes over the years but attributed them to aging and stress.
real_life_examples.first_change: His adult daughter insisted he seek evaluation when he forgot her birthday for the second year in a row and became confused about which grandchild was whose. His ex-wife mentioned he seemed like 'a different person' than the man she'd married twenty years ago.
real_life_examples.behaviors: Neuropsychological testing revealed significant memory deficits, executive function problems, and processing speed impairments. James frequently lost track of conversations mid-sentence, struggled to follow multi-step directions, and had difficulty with time perception—sometimes thinking hours had passed when it had been minutes. His emotional responses had become blunted and inappropriate. He'd had multiple arrests over the years for bizarre behavior during intoxication, including a incident where he was found wandering a highway at 3 AM, confused and disoriented. Recent episodes showed increasing paranoia even when not acutely intoxicated.
real_life_examples.consequences: James was diagnosed with both PCP use disorder and cognitive impairment likely related to chronic PCP use. He was deemed unable to live independently. He'd lost custody of his younger children years ago and had sporadic contact with his adult children. He was unemployed and receiving disability benefits.
real_life_examples.aftermath: James is in residential treatment and has been abstinent for four months, but his cognitive problems persist. Doctors are uncertain how much function he might recover. He's being evaluated for permanent cognitive impairment. His family is supportive but grieving the person he used to be. James himself struggles to remember what his life was like before PCP dominated it, and he's coming to terms with the possibility that some damage may be permanent. He's working on accepting his limitations while maximizing his remaining abilities.

real_life_examples.title: Unintended Exposure
real_life_examples.baseline: Tasha, 22, was a graduate student living with roommates. She occasionally smoked marijuana but was cautious about drugs. She was responsible, health-conscious, and had never had any psychiatric symptoms or behavioral problems.
real_life_examples.first_change: At a friend's apartment, she smoked what she thought was marijuana. Within minutes, she felt profoundly wrong—completely disconnected from reality and convinced the people around her were planning to hurt her. She experienced terrifying hallucinations and her body felt foreign.
real_life_examples.behaviors: Tasha locked herself in a bathroom, hearing voices telling her people were coming to kill her. She couldn't recognize her own reflection. Friends called through the door but she was convinced they were imposters. She began screaming and trying to break the mirror. When friends forced the door open, she fought them violently, something completely out of character. Her eyes showed rapid involuntary movements and she couldn't speak coherently. She didn't respond to her name and seemed unaware of pain when she cut her arm on mirror glass.
real_life_examples.consequences: Friends called an ambulance when they couldn't calm her. In the ER, Tasha remained severely agitated and paranoid for hours. Toxicology revealed PCP—someone had laced the marijuana without her knowledge. The episode was deeply traumatic. She developed severe anxiety about any substance use and had flashbacks to the terrifying hours of psychosis.
real_life_examples.aftermath: Despite being a one-time unintended exposure, Tasha continues therapy for the trauma of the experience. She has residual anxiety and panic attacks, especially triggered by anything related to that night. She's had to take time off from graduate school. The friend whose apartment it was lost contact with their drug supplier and has guilt about what happened. Tasha is learning that even a single PCP exposure can have lasting psychological impact, and she's working through her anger at being exposed to such a dangerous drug without consent.

comparisons.explanation: Both PCP and ketamine are dissociative anesthetics that block NMDA receptors, producing similar out-of-body experiences and dissociation. However, PCP is much longer-acting (effects lasting 4-6 hours or more vs. 45-90 minutes for ketamine) and has a higher risk of causing severe agitation and violence. PCP more commonly causes vertical nystagmus, while ketamine intoxication typically involves more sedation. Both can cause psychological dependence, but PCP use disorder is generally rarer and associated with more severe behavioral complications.

Both can cause severe agitation, psychotic symptoms (paranoia, hallucinations), and violent behavior during intoxication. However, methamphetamine is a stimulant that increases energy and decreases appetite, while PCP is a dissociative that causes more profound detachment from reality. Methamphetamine intoxication typically involves dilated pupils, while PCP characteristically causes nystagmus. Methamphetamine users often exhibit repetitive behaviors and extreme wakefulness, while PCP users show more unpredictable mood shifts and distinctive decreased pain sensitivity. Both disorders involve cravings and difficulty quitting.

PCP intoxication can produce symptoms nearly identical to schizophrenia—hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, and bizarre behavior. The key difference is timing: PCP-related symptoms are acute, time-linked to substance use, and typically resolve within hours to days, while schizophrenia symptoms are persistent, not substance-related, and show gradual onset. PCP users have distinctive physical signs (nystagmus, decreased pain response, ataxia) not present in schizophrenia. However, chronic heavy PCP use can cause lasting psychotic symptoms that blur this distinction, and some people with PCP use disorder also have co-occurring schizophrenia.

Both PCP and LSD are hallucinogens that alter perception and can cause visual disturbances and dissociative experiences. However, LSD is primarily a serotonergic hallucinogen causing vivid visual hallucinations and perceptual distortions, while PCP acts on NMDA receptors causing more profound dissociation and body disconnection. PCP is much more likely to cause aggression, violence, and dangerous behavior—LSD users typically remain aware they're experiencing drug effects (insight), while PCP users often lose touch with reality entirely. PCP causes distinctive physical signs like nystagmus and pain insensitivity not seen with LSD. True use disorders are rare for both, but PCP use carries higher risks of medical emergencies and violent behavior.

faqs.question: What is PCP and what does it do to your brain?
faqs.answer: PCP (phencyclidine) is a dissociative drug that was originally developed as an anesthetic. It works primarily by blocking NMDA receptors in the brain, which disrupts normal glutamate signaling. This causes feelings of detachment from one's body and environment, along with distorted perceptions. PCP also affects dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine systems, which can cause stimulant-like effects, mood changes, and psychosis-like symptoms. The combination of effects makes PCP uniquely dangerous—users may experience hallucinations, feel invincible, lose pain sensitivity, and behave unpredictably or violently.

faqs.question: How can you tell if someone is on PCP?
faqs.answer: PCP intoxication has distinctive signs: characteristic eye movements called nystagmus (rapid, involuntary eye movements, especially vertical), aggressive or unpredictable behavior that can switch suddenly, decreased response to pain (users may injure themselves without reacting), poor coordination and slurred speech, blank staring or dissociated appearance, and sometimes superhuman-seeming strength. Users may be paranoid, experience hallucinations, or show bizarre behavior. They often have elevated blood pressure and heart rate. The combination of dissociation, nystagmus, and decreased pain response is particularly characteristic of PCP rather than other substances.

faqs.question: Can you become addicted to PCP?
faqs.answer: Yes, regular PCP use can lead to a substance use disorder characterized by cravings, difficulty controlling use, continued use despite harmful consequences, and tolerance (needing more to achieve the same effects). While PCP doesn't cause the same physical withdrawal syndrome as alcohol or opioids, users develop psychological dependence and experience strong cravings. People often continue using despite negative consequences like arrests, injuries, relationship problems, or employment issues. The dissociative 'escape' PCP provides can be particularly reinforcing for people dealing with trauma or psychological pain.

faqs.question: Is PCP dangerous? What are the risks?
faqs.answer: PCP is extremely dangerous for multiple reasons. Immediate risks include violent or self-destructive behavior (users may hurt themselves or others without awareness), life-threatening injuries from not feeling pain or believing they're invincible, medical emergencies like seizures, extremely high blood pressure, or hyperthermia, psychotic symptoms including terrifying hallucinations and paranoia, and accidents due to severely impaired coordination and judgment. Long-term risks include persistent cognitive problems (memory, attention, processing speed), lasting psychiatric symptoms, physical injuries from intoxicated behavior, legal consequences from aggressive or bizarre behavior, and potential permanent neurological damage with chronic use.

faqs.question: How long do PCP effects last?
faqs.answer: PCP effects typically begin within 2-5 minutes when smoked and 30-60 minutes when taken orally. The acute intoxication phase usually lasts 4-6 hours but can persist much longer with high doses—sometimes 24-48 hours. Physical effects and psychological symptoms gradually diminish but users may experience confusion, memory problems, or mood changes for days afterward. Chronic users may develop persistent cognitive and psychiatric symptoms that continue between uses. The duration is significantly longer than similar dissociatives like ketamine, which is one factor that makes PCP particularly dangerous.

faqs.question: What should you do if someone is having a bad reaction to PCP?
faqs.answer: Call 911 immediately. PCP intoxication can be a medical emergency. While waiting for help: prioritize safety—remove dangerous objects and keep a safe distance if the person is aggressive, don't try to physically restrain them unless absolutely necessary as this can escalate agitation, keep the environment calm and quiet (loud noises or bright lights can worsen agitation), don't leave them alone, and protect them from self-harm. Medical treatment may include benzodiazepines for severe agitation, monitoring of vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature), and supportive care. Do not try to 'talk them down'—they likely can't process information normally while intoxicated.

faqs.question: Can PCP cause permanent damage?
faqs.answer: Yes, PCP can cause lasting effects, especially with chronic use. Research shows persistent cognitive impairments including memory problems, decreased attention span, difficulty with problem-solving and executive functions, and slower processing speed. Some users develop ongoing psychiatric symptoms like paranoia, depression, or psychotic symptoms even when not using. Brain imaging studies suggest possible long-term changes in brain structure and function. There may also be permanent physical damage from injuries sustained during intoxication (broken bones, head injuries). However, some cognitive function may improve with sustained abstinence, and the extent of recovery varies by individual and use history.

faqs.question: Why do people become violent on PCP?
faqs.answer: PCP's effects on multiple brain systems create conditions for aggression and violence: the drug disrupts normal perception and thinking, so users may misinterpret others' intentions as threatening; it reduces pain sensitivity and can create feelings of invincibility, removing normal deterrents to aggression; it affects dopamine and other systems in ways that increase impulsivity and reduce behavioral control; users often experience paranoia and may feel they're defending themselves from perceived threats; and the profound dissociation means users aren't fully aware of their actions or consequences. Not all PCP users become violent, but the risk is significant enough that PCP intoxication is a psychiatric emergency.

faqs.question: What's the difference between PCP intoxication and PCP use disorder?
faqs.answer: PCP intoxication refers to the acute state of being under the influence of PCP—the behavioral changes, physical signs, and psychological symptoms that occur during and shortly after using the drug. It's a temporary condition that resolves as the drug leaves the system. PCP use disorder is a pattern of problematic use over time characterized by impaired control over use, continued use despite negative consequences, cravings, tolerance, and interference with responsibilities. Someone can experience intoxication without having a use disorder (such as a first-time user or someone exposed without consent), or they may have a use disorder that includes repeated episodes of intoxication along with ongoing issues controlling their use.

faqs.question: How is PCP different from angel dust?
faqs.answer: They're the same substance—'angel dust' is a street name for PCP (phencyclidine). Other street names include 'wet,' 'sherm,' 'rocket fuel,' 'embalming fluid,' and 'peace pill.' PCP is sometimes sold as powder ('angel dust') that can be snorted or mixed with tobacco or marijuana for smoking. The drug may also come as pills, capsules, or liquid. Regardless of the name or form, it's the same dangerous dissociative drug. The variety of street names can make it harder to know what substance someone has actually used, which is why specific toxicology testing is often needed to identify PCP.

faqs.question: Can you test for PCP use?
faqs.answer: Yes, but PCP testing requires specific screening—it's not always included in standard drug tests. PCP can be detected in urine typically for 7-14 days after use in occasional users, and potentially longer (up to 30 days) in chronic heavy users. It can also be detected in blood, saliva, and hair. However, many employers' standard 5-panel drug tests don't include PCP, which means use can be missed. If PCP intoxication is suspected clinically (based on symptoms like nystagmus, behavior, and vital signs), doctors can order specific PCP testing. This is one reason PCP use is sometimes missed in initial evaluations—it has to be specifically looked for.

faqs.question: What treatment is available for PCP use disorder?
faqs.answer: Treatment typically involves comprehensive substance abuse treatment including: behavioral therapies like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) to identify triggers and develop coping strategies, motivational interviewing to address ambivalence about quitting, and contingency management providing rewards for maintaining abstinence. There are currently no FDA-approved medications specifically for PCP use disorder, but treatment may include medications for co-occurring conditions like depression or anxiety. Treatment also addresses any cognitive deficits through cognitive rehabilitation, provides peer support through groups like NA, and includes relapse prevention planning. For people who have experienced PCP-related trauma or violence, trauma-informed care is important. Success requires addressing the underlying reasons someone was using PCP.

faqs.question: PCP vs ketamine: What's the difference?
faqs.answer: Both are dissociative anesthetics that block NMDA receptors and produce out-of-body experiences, but they differ significantly. Duration: PCP effects last 4-6+ hours while ketamine lasts 45-90 minutes. Behavioral effects: PCP much more commonly causes severe agitation, unpredictability, and violence, while ketamine typically causes more sedation. Medical use: Ketamine is still used as an anesthetic and for treatment-resistant depression; PCP is not used medically. Controllability: Ketamine's shorter duration allows more control over the experience; PCP's long duration can lead to prolonged dangerous states. Safety profile: While both carry risks, PCP is generally considered more dangerous due to longer duration, greater unpredictability, and higher association with violent behavior.

faqs.question: PCP vs methamphetamine: How can you tell them apart?
faqs.answer: Both can cause agitation, paranoia, and violent behavior, but they have distinct features. Eye signs: PCP causes nystagmus (rapid involuntary eye movements), especially vertical, while methamphetamine causes dilated pupils. Energy level: Methamphetamine is a stimulant causing extreme wakefulness and energy, while PCP causes more dissociation and unpredictable shifts between agitation and stupor. Pain response: PCP users have notably decreased pain sensitivity; this is not characteristic of methamphetamine. Duration: Methamphetamine effects last 8-12 hours with prolonged wakefulness; PCP intoxication is typically shorter but with more severe acute behavioral changes. Physically: Methamphetamine use often shows repetitive behaviors and jaw clenching; PCP shows more ataxia and muscle rigidity.

faqs.question: PCP vs schizophrenia: How can doctors tell the difference?
faqs.answer: This is challenging because PCP intoxication can look almost identical to a schizophrenia psychotic episode, with hallucinations, delusions, and bizarre behavior. Key distinguishing factors: Timeline—PCP symptoms are acute with sudden onset after substance use and resolve within hours to days; schizophrenia develops gradually and symptoms persist. Physical signs—PCP causes nystagmus, elevated blood pressure, decreased pain response, and ataxia not present in schizophrenia. Toxicology—specific testing can detect PCP in the system. History—is there a known pattern of substance use? Prior episodes? However, complications include: PCP isn't always tested for, the person may not disclose use, chronic PCP use can cause lasting psychotic symptoms, and some people have both schizophrenia and substance use disorder. When in doubt, substance-induced psychosis is often assumed until proven otherwise.

faqs.question: Why isn't PCP more common if it's so powerful?
faqs.answer: Several factors limit PCP use despite its potent effects: the high risk of extremely negative experiences (terrifying hallucinations, loss of control, violent behavior), cultural reputation as one of the most dangerous street drugs, difficulty in production compared to some other substances, and geographic concentration (use is not evenly distributed and may be more common in certain regions and subcultures). The unpredictability of effects—users can't control whether they'll have a 'good trip' or a terrifying, dangerous experience—makes it less appealing than substances with more predictable effects. Additionally, the long duration and severity of intoxication can be off-putting. Most substance users seek some form of pleasurable or controllable experience, and PCP's reputation for causing bizarre and dangerous behavior serves as a deterrent.

faqs.question: Can you overdose on PCP?
faqs.answer: Yes, PCP overdose can be life-threatening. High doses can cause seizures, severely elevated blood pressure and heart rate, dangerous hyperthermia (overheating), respiratory depression, coma, and stroke or cardiac arrest. Death can also result from behavioral effects—injuries from violence or accidents, dangerous decisions while believing one is invincible, or complications from prolonged agitation. There's no specific antidote for PCP overdose, so treatment is supportive: managing agitation with sedatives, cooling for hyperthermia, treating seizures, and monitoring vital functions. The unpredictable potency of street PCP (which may be mixed with other substances) makes dosing difficult and overdose risk significant, especially for people who are using for the first time or after a period of abstinence.

faqs.question: What happens to your body during PCP withdrawal?
faqs.answer: Unlike alcohol or opioids, PCP doesn't produce a severe or dangerous physical withdrawal syndrome. However, people who stop chronic PCP use often experience psychological withdrawal that can be challenging: intense drug cravings, depression or dysphoria, fatigue and sleep disturbances, anxiety and irritability, and sometimes flashbacks or brief psychotic symptoms. Cognitive difficulties may persist (trouble concentrating, memory problems). Some users report feeling disoriented or having difficulty reconnecting with reality. These symptoms typically peak within the first week but can persist for weeks to months. While not medically dangerous, the psychological discomfort and cravings are significant barriers to quitting. Treatment focuses on supportive care, addressing mood symptoms, and intensive behavioral support during this vulnerable period.

faqs.question: Why would someone use PCP knowing how dangerous it is?
faqs.answer: People use PCP for various reasons despite the risks: some are seeking the dissociative escape from reality, physical pain, or emotional distress; others are drawn by curiosity or peer influence without fully understanding the dangers; some people inadvertently use it (PCP may be used to lace marijuana or other substances without users' knowledge); and individuals with existing substance use disorders may have impaired risk assessment. For those who continue use after initial exposure, the powerful dissociative effects can be reinforcing, especially for people dealing with trauma, chronic pain, or mental health issues. Once a pattern develops, cravings and psychological dependence make quitting difficult despite awareness of risks. Additionally, misinformation or minimization of dangers within certain social groups can influence continued use.

faqs.question: How do I know if my marijuana might be laced with PCP?
faqs.answer: Unfortunately, it's very difficult to tell by appearance alone. Warning signs that might indicate PCP-laced marijuana include: unusual chemical smell (PCP can have a distinctive chemical or ether-like odor), marijuana that seems unusually wet or oily, being offered marijuana from unfamiliar sources or described with unusual street names like 'wet,' 'fry,' or 'sherm,' and marijuana sold at unusually low prices. The only certain way to know is through chemical testing. If you use marijuana, reduce risks by: obtaining it from reliable, legal sources where possible, being cautious about trying marijuana from new or unknown sources, never using alone when trying a new supply, and knowing the signs of PCP intoxication so you can seek help immediately if they occur. Most importantly, if you experience profound dissociation, nystagmus, or severe behavioral changes after using marijuana, seek emergency medical care.

content.when_to_seek_help: Immediate medical attention if severe agitation, psychosis, seizures, or unresponsiveness occur; prompt evaluation for any ongoing PCP use or related behavioral incidents.
